textContent.text: Gregor Mendel, an Austrian monk and scientist, was born on July 20, 1822. He conducted experimental studies on pea plants in his monastery's garden that would prove to be foundational to modern genetics. Mendel's studies established many rules of heredity, known today as the laws of Mendelian inheritance.

pieces.text: In 1866, Mendel published a paper asserting that parents transmit distinct "heritable factors," now known as

, to their offspring. He correctly argued that these factors maintain their identity across generations. In other words, Mendel claimed genes are like a deck of playing cards. Even if you shuffle and sort them, each card maintains its individuality. The cards never blend together. This countered the popular theory of

, which proposed that parents' traits were averaged together to form the characteristics of their offspring. Though Mendel's work was largely overlooked during his lifetime, its rediscovery in the early 1900s led to numerous significant scientific advances. Today, Mendel is considered the father of modern genetics.

pieces.text: Gregor Mendel chose the garden pea plant,
, as the experimental organism for his studies. This species was an ideal experimental organism for many reasons:

elements.text: It typically self-pollinates, so cross-pollination could be easily controlled for experimental genetic crosses.
It reproduces and matures rapidly, so Mendel could track traits over many generations relatively quickly.
Each genetic cross produces many offspring, so Mendel's studies had large sample sizes with statistical reliability.
Its traits are easy to identify and track over time because they each have two contrasting forms and can be observed with the naked eye.

textContent.text: Gregor Mendel, an Austrian monk and scientist, was born on July 20, 1822. He conducted experimental studies on pea plants in his monastery's garden that would prove to be foundational to modern genetics. Mendel's studies established many rules of heredity, known today as the laws of Mendelian inheritance.

pieces.text: In 1866, Mendel published a paper asserting that parents transmit distinct "heritable factors," now known as

, to their offspring. He correctly argued that these factors maintain their identity across generations. In other words, Mendel claimed genes are like a deck of playing cards. Even if you shuffle and sort them, each card maintains its individuality. The cards never blend together. This countered the popular theory of

, which proposed that parents' traits were averaged together to form the characteristics of their offspring. Though Mendel's work was largely overlooked during his lifetime, its rediscovery in the early 1900s led to numerous significant scientific advances. Today, Mendel is considered the father of modern genetics.

textContent.text: Gregor Mendel, an Austrian monk and scientist, was born on July 20, 1822. He conducted experimental studies on pea plants in his monastery's garden that would prove to be foundational to modern genetics. Mendel's studies established many rules of heredity, known today as the laws of Mendelian inheritance.

pieces.text: In 1866, Mendel published a paper asserting that parents transmit distinct "heritable factors," now known as

, to their offspring. He correctly argued that these factors maintain their identity across generations. In other words, Mendel claimed genes are like a deck of playing cards. Even if you shuffle and sort them, each card maintains its individuality. The cards never blend together. This countered the popular theory of

, which proposed that parents' traits were averaged together to form the characteristics of their offspring. Though Mendel's work was largely overlooked during his lifetime, its rediscovery in the early 1900s led to numerous significant scientific advances. Today, Mendel is considered the father of modern genetics.

textContent.text: Gregor Mendel, an Austrian monk and scientist, was born on July 20, 1822. He conducted experimental studies on pea plants in his monastery's garden that would prove to be foundational to modern genetics. Mendel's studies established many rules of heredity, known today as the laws of Mendelian inheritance.

pieces.text: In 1866, Mendel published a paper asserting that parents transmit distinct "heritable factors," now known as

, to their offspring. He correctly argued that these factors maintain their identity across generations. In other words, Mendel claimed genes are like a deck of playing cards. Even if you shuffle and sort them, each card maintains its individuality. The cards never blend together. This countered the popular theory of

, which proposed that parents' traits were averaged together to form the characteristics of their offspring. Though Mendel's work was largely overlooked during his lifetime, its rediscovery in the early 1900s led to numerous significant scientific advances. Today, Mendel is considered the father of modern genetics.

Plants that produce a high level of chlorophyll in the rind have green fruit. Some plants do not produce chlorophyll in the rind and have white fruit.

pieces.text: In a group of eggplants, some plants have green fruit, some have white fruit, and some have light-green fruit. Fruit color is dependent on chlorophyll production. In this group, the gene for chlorophyll production in the rind has two alleles. The allele for chlorophyll production that results in green fruit (
) is incompletely dominant over the allele for no production that results in white fruit (
). So heterozygotes have light-green fruit.

pieces.text: Human DNA is packaged into discrete units called chromosomes. Humans inherit 23 pairs of chromosomes from their parents, which each contain unique genes that determine traits and help the body function. Of these pairs, 22 are called
. They contain the vast majority of a person's genetic information.
The chromosomes that make up the 23rd pair are known as

because they contain genes that define an individual's biological sex. There are two kinds of sex chromosomes in humans: X and Y. An individual who inherits two X chromosomes is typically female, while an individual who inherits one X chromosome and one Y chromosome is typically male.

contents.text: Because males have only one X chromosome, they express whichever allele they inherit for an X-linked gene, even if it is recessive.

For example, the genes responsible for making the eye's light-sensitive pigments are X-linked. A mutated recessive allele for one of these genes causes red-green color blindness. Since females typically have two X chromosomes, they will only be red-green colorblind if they inherit two copies of the recessive allele. But since males typically have only one X chromosome, they need only inherit one copy of the mutated gene to be red-green colorblind.
